title: Level 6: Timer1 in CTC Mode — Precision 1 Hz Signal Generation
aim: To configure the ATmega328P's 16-bit Timer1 in Clear Timer on Compare Match (CTC) mode to generate a precise, hardware-driven 1 Hz LED toggle without software counters.
objective: Understand Timer1's 16-bit architecture, the CTC waveform generation mode, OCR1A as the programmable TOP value, the TIMSK1 Compare Match interrupt, and compute exact OCR1A values from frequency specifications.
theory:
Timer1 — The 16-Bit Timer

Where Timer0 is 8 bits (0–255), Timer1 is a full 16-bit timer/counter — its register pair TCNT1H:TCNT1L can count from 0 to 65,535 (0xFFFF). This 256× larger count range allows much longer timing intervals without an overflow counter. At 16 MHz and ÷1024 prescaler, Timer1 overflows every 65,536 × 64 µs ≈ 4.19 seconds.

Normal Mode vs CTC Mode

In Normal Mode (Timer0, Exp 5), the timer counts to 255/65535 and overflows — you need a software counter to count overflows for longer periods. CTC (Clear Timer on Compare match) Mode solves this directly: the timer compares its count against the value in OCR1A (Output Compare Register 1A). The instant TCNT1 == OCR1A, the hardware automatically clears TCNT1 back to 0 and fires the Compare Match A interrupt. The timer period is entirely determined by the OCR1A value.

Calculating the OCR1A Value

The formula for CTC period is:

OCR1A = (f_cpu / (prescaler × f_target)) − 1

For a 1 Hz interrupt at 16 MHz with ÷1024 prescaler:

OCR1A = (16,000,000 / (1024 × 1)) − 1 = 15,625 − 1 = 15,624

This is exact — no approximation needed, no software counter required. Set OCR1A = 15624; and the hardware generates a precise 1 Hz interrupt automatically.

Timer1 Register Configuration

  • TCCR1A — Control Register A. For CTC mode via OCR1A, both WGM1x bits in TCCR1A are 0 (Normal/CTC mode depends on WGM13:WGM10 combination). In CTC Mode 4: WGM13=0, WGM12=1, WGM11=0, WGM10=0.
  • TCCR1B — Control Register B. Holds WGM12 (bit 3) and CS1x prescaler bits. Setting WGM12=1 and CS12=1, CS10=1 (÷1024) simultaneously sets CTC mode and starts the timer.
  • OCR1A — 16-bit compare register. Write the computed count value. Hardware auto-clears TCNT1 when it matches.
  • TIMSK1 — Interrupt Mask. Set OCIE1A (Output Compare Interrupt Enable 1A, bit 1) to enable the Compare Match A interrupt.

Interrupt Vector

The Compare Match A ISR is declared as ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect). Unlike the overflow ISR in Exp 5, you do not need a counter variable — the ISR runs at exactly 1 Hz by design. Simply toggle the LED immediately in the ISR.

Why CTC is Superior for Fixed-Frequency Applications

CTC eliminates the software overhead of counting overflows, reduces interrupt frequency by up to 256×, and provides exact frequency generation with zero jitter (assuming stable crystal). The hardware handles the full timing — the CPU is only woken for the final action.

pretest.question: What is the maximum count value of Timer1 (16-bit timer)?
pretest.explanation: A 16-bit counter holds values 0 through 2^16−1 = 65,535. This allows 256× more granularity than the 8-bit Timer0.

pretest.question: In CTC mode, what happens when TCNT1 equals OCR1A?
options: TCNT1 is automatically cleared to 0 and Compare Match interrupt fires
pretest.explanation: CTC (Clear Timer on Compare match): TCNT1 is hardware-cleared to 0 on match, and if OCIE1A is set, the TIMER1_COMPA_vect ISR is triggered.

pretest.question: Using OCR1A = (F_CPU / (prescaler × frequency)) − 1 for 1 Hz at 16 MHz ÷1024, what is OCR1A?
pretest.explanation: OCR1A = (16,000,000 / (1024 × 1)) − 1 = 15,625 − 1 = 15,624. Exact integer — no software counting needed.

pretest.question: Which bit in TCCR1B enables CTC mode with OCR1A as TOP?
pretest.explanation: CTC Mode 4 is selected by WGM13:WGM12:WGM11:WGM10 = 0:1:0:0. WGM12 in TCCR1B is the critical bit to set. WGM13, WGM11, WGM10 remain 0.

pretest.question: Which bit in TIMSK1 enables the Timer1 Compare Match A interrupt?
pretest.explanation: OCIE1A (Output Compare 1A Interrupt Enable, bit 1) in TIMSK1 enables the interrupt that fires when TCNT1 reaches OCR1A in CTC mode.

pretest.question: What is the name of the Timer1 Compare Match A ISR vector?
pretest.explanation: TIMER1_COMPA_vect is the interrupt vector for Timer1 Compare Match A. This is triggered when TCNT1 == OCR1A in CTC mode.

pretest.question: Why does CTC mode require no software overflow counter (unlike Normal mode)?
options: OCR1A acts as a programmable TOP — the hardware generates exactly the desired period
pretest.explanation: In Normal mode, you count 61 overflows to reach 1 second. In CTC, you set OCR1A=15624 and the hardware directly generates 1 Hz — no counter variable needed.

pretest.question: How are the two bytes of the 16-bit OCR1A register written safely?
options: Write as a 16-bit word; AVR handles byte order automatically
Use only the low byte OCR1AL
pretest.explanation: On AVR, 16-bit registers like OCR1A are accessed as a 16-bit type in C. The compiler generates the correct sequence (high byte buffered, low byte triggers update).

pretest.question: At 16 MHz with ÷1024 prescaler, what is the Timer1 tick period?
pretest.explanation: Tick period = prescaler / F_CPU = 1024 / 16,000,000 = 64 µs per tick.

pretest.question: What is the purpose of sei() after configuring the timer?
options: Enables the global interrupt I-bit in SREG so the Compare Match ISR can fire
pretest.explanation: sei() sets the I-bit in SREG. Without it, all interrupts including TIMER1_COMPA are masked at the global level regardless of individual TIMSK1 settings.

procedure: Include headers: #include <avr/io.h> and #include <avr/interrupt.h>. Define #define LED_PIN PB5. No delay or stdio headers needed.
Set Timer1 to CTC Mode 4. In TCCR1A, both WGM bits are 0 (keep default). In TCCR1B, set WGM12 to enable CTC mode: TCCR1B |= (1 << WGM12);.
Set the prescaler to ÷1024 by writing CS12 and CS10 in TCCR1B: TCCR1B |= (1 << CS12) | (1 << CS10);. This simultaneously starts the timer. The timer is now running in CTC mode with ÷1024 clock.

Calculate and load the compare value. For a 1 Hz interrupt: OCR1A = (16000000 / (1024 × 1)) − 1 = 15624. Write it: OCR1A = 15624;. The hardware will fire the Compare Match interrupt every time TCNT1 reaches this value and then clear TCNT1.
Enable the Timer1 Compare Match A interrupt: TIMSK1 |= (1 << OCIE1A);. This arms the Compare Match interrupt — it will fire every 1 second.
Enable global interrupts: sei();. The timer is fully operational.

Leave the main loop empty: while(1) {}. Write the ISR: ISR(TIMER1_COMPA_vect) { PORTB ^= (1 << LED_PIN); }. The LED toggles exactly once per second with hardware-level precision and no software counter variable.

posttest.question: To generate a 2 Hz interrupt instead of 1 Hz, what OCR1A value should be used?
posttest.explanation: For 2 Hz: OCR1A = (16,000,000 / (1024 × 2)) − 1 = 7812.5 − 1 ≈ 7812. This halves the period to 500 ms, giving 2 toggles per second.

posttest.question: What happens to TCNT1 when it matches OCR1A in CTC mode?
options: Is cleared back to 0 by hardware
posttest.explanation: CTC = Clear Timer on Compare match. TCNT1 is automatically reset to 0 by the hardware the cycle after the match, creating a perfectly periodic waveform.

posttest.question: If you used the ÷256 prescaler instead of ÷1024, what OCR1A value gives 1 Hz?
posttest.explanation: OCR1A = (16,000,000 / (256 × 1)) − 1 = 62,500 − 1 = 62,499. This is within the 16-bit range (max 65,535) so it's valid.

posttest.question: What advantage does Timer1 have over Timer0 for precision timing?
options: Timer1's 16-bit counter allows longer periods and finer resolution
posttest.explanation: Timer1's 16-bit range (0–65535) vs Timer0's 8-bit (0–255) means 256× more resolution — enabling exact timing for longer periods without software counter overhead.

posttest.question: Which TCCR1B bit arrangement gives ÷1024 prescaler?
posttest.explanation: Per the ATmega328P datasheet Table 15-6: CS12=1, CS11=0, CS10=1 selects clk_IO/1024 prescaler for Timer1.

posttest.question: What is the SREG register?
options: Status Register holding CPU flags (Carry, Zero, Overflow, I-bit etc.)
posttest.explanation: SREG (Status Register) is an 8-bit register holding arithmetic flags (C,Z,N,V,S,H,T) and the global interrupt enable I-bit.

posttest.question: What does the SREG register contain?
options: Status Register with CPU flags and I-bit
posttest.explanation: SREG holds CPU flags and the global interrupt enable bit (I-bit, bit 7).

posttest.question: In an ISR, interrupts are automatically:
options: Disabled until ISR returns (RETI restores I-bit)
posttest.explanation: The AVR clears the I-bit in SREG on ISR entry, preventing nested interrupts. RETI restores it.

posttest.question: Which is NOT a valid ATmega328P port?
posttest.explanation: ATmega328P has only Port B, C, D. No Port A exists.

posttest.question: What is a watchdog timer used for?
posttest.explanation: If firmware fails to periodically clear the WDT within its timeout window, the WDT forces a system reset to recover from hangs or crashes.

feedback: Flawless! CTC mode is the workhorse of precision timing — sound generation, motor control step rates, servo signalling, and communication protocols all depend on exactly what you built here.
